source: Steele, Wen & Han (2026) One mechanism for many mental spaces (re-read for gaps 4 and 6)
finding: Re-read for K04 and K25. The report-versus-use split is shown only by subspace interventions on open models of 3B or less. No prompt-level test (such as an explicit apply-the-rule step) is reported. The belief companion paper is by the same group, so belief-not-special has no independent replication.
numbers: Report subspace flips colour 1.00 but the rule consequent only 0.49 on Falcon3 (0.29 for the reasoning subspace on colour); mean principal cosine 0.11 Qwen, 0.17 Falcon3. Pythia-2.8b cannot apply the rule (baseline near chance), so the test is uninterpretable there. Frontier models (gpt-4o, Qwen2.5-72B, Gemini-2.5) hold eight spaces with no swap errors.
quote: A faithfulness failure is, on this account, an intervention on one subspace that leaves the other untouched.
limits: Authors say the two most specific causal claims have the narrowest support. Companion belief paper is cited as Steele et al. 2026 and was not found as a separate record. The paper links the report/use gap to CoT faithfulness work (Turpin 2023, Lanham 2023) but runs no prompting test.
agent_relevance: Gap 4 stays open: no evidence that a prompt step closes the report-use gap. Treat 'apply the rule inside space X' as an untested design guess to measure.

source: Zhu, Zhang & Wang (2024) Language Models Represent Beliefs of Self and Others
finding: Independent group. Belief status of self and other agents is linearly decodable from Mistral-7B-Instruct attention heads, and steering those heads changes ToM accuracy a lot. Steering helps forward belief far more than backward belief.
numbers: BigToM Table 1, Mistral-7B with joint-belief steering (+TpFo): Forward Belief TB/FB/Both 0.99/0.98/0.97; Forward Action 0.98/0.81/0.79; Backward Belief 0.86/0.53/0.40. Probes: heads above 75% validation accuracy on binary belief status (random 50%). Reference rows: GPT-4 Backward Belief Both 0.33, Claude 0.40, GPT-3.5 0.24. Table text was garbled in extraction; the Mistral baseline row was not read reliably.
limits: One 7B model for steering; BigToM is synthetic; no comparison with a prompt-level scaffold.
agent_relevance: Supports K20 and K14 from a second group: backward inference stays near 0.40 even when forward is 0.97 after steering. A hypothesis-first step is not tested here.

source: Bortoletto, Ruhdorfer, Shi & Bulling (2024) Brittle Minds, Fixable Activations
finding: Belief representations in LMs are structured (not spurious) and improve with model size and fine-tuning, but change with prompt wording. Activation edits can correct wrong ToM inferences.
numbers: Abstract page only; it gave no numbers and did not name the models.
agent_relevance: A second independent group on belief representations (with Zhu et al.). Brittleness to prompt variation argues for one fixed, repeated scope-tag format rather than free wording.

source: Reasoning vs non-reasoning models on theory of mind (arXiv 2602.10625, 'To Think or Not To Think')
finding: On HiToM, ToMATO and ToMBench, reasoning models do not consistently beat non-reasoning ones and sometimes do worse. Overall HiToM: GPT-o3 0.747 best, DeepSeek-V3 0.694, Qwen3-32B-Reasoning 0.680, GPT-4o 0.607, Qwen3-32B 0.586, Qwen3-8B 0.558, DeepSeek-R1 0.549, GPT-o4-mini 0.547, Qwen3-8B-Reasoning 0.481.
numbers: 9 models (5 reasoning, 4 non-reasoning). Max output 2,048 tokens, temperature 0. N not stated in the text read.
quote: reasoning models do not consistently outperform non-reasoning models and sometimes perform worse
limits: Only the first 100,000 of 104,911 characters were read.
agent_relevance: Answers gap 2 for 2025-2026 models: more thinking alone does not fix scoped belief tracking.

source: Same paper (2602.10625), Table 3: HiToM accuracy by nesting order
finding: Accuracy falls with nesting order for most models, but not smoothly and not for all. DeepSeek-V3 stays near 0.6 from order 2 to 4. GPT-o3 is the best reasoning model at order 4.
limits: Order 3 and 4 are well above the near-zero of the original Hi-ToM paper for several models, so the collapse is partly closed for 2025-2026 models, but order 4 is still 0.2 to 0.6. No explicit-stack condition.
agent_relevance: Gap 8: depth still costs 0.4 to 0.8 points for most current models. K13 should say 'falls but not to zero' for current models. A written stack of spaces was not tested here.

source: Same paper (2602.10625): fixes tried on HiToM
finding: Removing multiple-choice options helps reasoning models. Early stopping of 'wait' loops and capping tokens also help. CoT helps non-reasoning models.
numbers: DeepSeek-R1 0.549 to 0.691 without options; Qwen3-8B-Reasoning 0.481 to 0.629; Qwen3-8B non-reasoning 0.557 to 0.510. Slow-to-Fast (stop at 3 'wait'): Qwen3-8B 0.481 to 0.557, R1-Distill-Qwen-32B 0.571 to 0.701, Qwen3-32B 0.680 to 0.682. Token cap 1,500 on Qwen3-8B-Reasoning: 0.706. CoT: DeepSeek-V3 0.665 to 0.723; Qwen3-32B 0.525 to 0.647.
limits: Token costs of baselines not reported; open-source models only for S2F and cap. Think-to-Match gains only shown in a figure.
agent_relevance: Over-long thinking can hurt scoped reasoning. A step budget is supported; unbounded deliberation is not.

source: de Haan, van der Putten & van Duijn (2026) Reasoning Promotes Robustness in Theory of Mind Tasks
finding: Reasoning models (GPT-5, Claude thinking, Grok-3-mini, R1, o1) handle Sally-Anne variants, Strange Stories and Imposing Memories near ceiling and are more robust to prompt changes. Authors argue the gain is more reliable convergence on a solution models could already reach with prompting, not new ToM.
numbers: Claude with thinking 100% vs 92% non-thinking on the memories test. Strange stories close to perfect for GPT-5. Very small item counts per cell (scores in steps of 0.5 or 1.0).
quote: models even sometimes display a version of what the perspective-taking prompting technique tries to achieve without being provoked
limits: Tiny samples; temperature 0; reasoning summaries differ by vendor; authors admit the comparison is not perfectly controlled and that models may recognise the classic test. Benchmark Table 6 is copied from another paper.
agent_relevance: Partly answers gap 2: base ToM scoping is now near ceiling for current models, so a SimToM-style filter has little room on classic items. Hard cases remain.

source: de Haan et al. (2026): trivial-alteration tasks (Table 5)
finding: Ullman-style alterations: transparent container (2A) and relationship change (2B) are still failed by most current models even with reasoning, while other alterations pass.
numbers: Scores on 2A.1/2A.2/2B.1/2B.2: Claude 0/0/0/0; Grok-3-mini 0/0/0/0; R1 0/0/0/0; GPT-5-high 0.5/0.5/0/0; non-reasoning Claude 0/0/0/0. Other alterations (1A-1D, 2C) mostly 1.0 for reasoning models; non-reasoning Claude 0.5 on several.
limits: Two items per cell. Authors argue 2A and 2B are not trivial because they need a visual mental picture.
agent_relevance: K11 stays contested: robustness is better, but a scene-visibility alteration still breaks scoped belief. Spaces need an explicit visibility step, not only a believer tag.

finding: RL on belief tracking (3,200 questions, orders up to 3) lifts Qwen2.5 models strongly on order 4, which was held out. Models of 3B and smaller shorten their reasoning (shortcuts); 7B-1M stays stable.
numbers: Hi-ToM overall N=600: Qwen2.5-7B 52.17 to 83.33; 3B 39.17 to 81.17; 0.5B 30.33 to 70.83. Order 4 (N=600, held out): 7B-1M 17.83 to 94.50; 7B 28.83 to 82.83; baselines DeepSeek-V3 58.67, GPT-4o 46.17, GPT-4o-mini 30.50. Response length of 1.5B fell 88.4% while accuracy rose.
limits: Training, not prompting. The authors' shortcut reading is interpretation, not a tested result. Generator templates may overlap between train and test.
agent_relevance: Depth collapse is trainable but that is not our route (no training). Shows the collapse is not a hard limit of nesting.

source: Kim et al. (2025, COLM) Hypothesis-Driven Theory-of-Mind Reasoning (thought-tracing)
finding: An inference-time method keeps weighted hypotheses about one agent's mental state at each step (a scoped space per agent with several rival hypotheses), updates weights by how likely the observed action is, and beats plain CoT on four ToM benchmarks. It is the closest found test of scoped hypotheses against flat reasoning, but only for ToM.
numbers: GPT-4o: ParaphrasedToMi 59.5 plain, 67.0 CoT, 76.0 TT, 74.3 TT+CoT; FANToM all-questions 11.1 / 40.7 / 41.5 / 54.7; MMToM avg 56.5 / 56.0 / 60.0 / 69.0. Llama-3.3-70B ToMi 57.3 / 64.5 / 71.3 / 77.0. Gemini-1.5-Pro ToMi 54.8 / 58.3 / 74.3 / 61.5. Qwen2.5-72B: TT alone gave no FANToM gain (0.0 to 1.9) but TT+CoT 32.1. BigToM re-annotated by 510 raters, 249 items kept (agreement above 90%).
quote: ThoughtTracing (+TT) improves all baseline models across all benchmarks.
limits: GPT-4o and Gemini: TT+CoT worse than TT alone on ToMi (true-belief cases degrade). Table extraction partly garbled for some rows. Compares with flat CoT, not with a flat hypothesis list at equal tokens.
agent_relevance: Gap 1 partly: scoped, weighted hypotheses beat flat CoT in ToM at similar or lower token cost, but there is no multi-hypothesis test outside ToM. Gap 10: generating rival hypotheses before matching observations is the core move.

source: Kim et al. (2025): thought-tracing versus reasoning models and token cost
finding: Reasoning models are strong on false belief but weak on true belief (they over-assume a false belief). Thought-tracing with a non-reasoning model matches or beats them using fewer tokens.
numbers: ParaphrasedToMi false/true belief: o1-medium 96.0/45.5; o1-high 97.0/49.0; o1-low 98.5/37.0; R1 77.0/59.5; GPT-4o+TT 84.5/67.5. Avg: o1-high 73.0, R1 68.3, o3-mini-medium 64.0, GPT-4o+TT 76.0. MMToM-QA: R1 49.0, o3-mini-medium 69.0, o1-high 76.5, GPT-4o+TT+CoT 69.0 with under 50% of o3-mini-medium tokens. FANToM all-Qs: o3-mini-medium 0.0, o1-high 37.9, R1 37.9. Output tokens of o1 and o3-mini do not track accuracy; ToM questions draw more tokens than factual ones.
limits: Token counts are in a figure, not read as numbers. 'Under 50%' is the authors' statement.
agent_relevance: Answers gap 2 partly: a scoped scaffold beats native reasoning models at lower token cost on these benchmarks, with 2025 models. Over-separation (treating shared knowledge as false belief) is a real failure of scoping.

finding: Removing perception inference hurts most; uniform hypothesis weights hurt slightly; adding self-correction of earlier hypotheses does not help.
numbers: Score change vs full TT (ToMi / FANToM / MMToM): GPT-4o without perception -16.2 / -17.0 / -7.0; without weight update -4.2 / 0.0 / -4.0; with self-correction -4.2 / -3.8 / -4.0. Llama-3.3-70B without perception -12.8 / -9.4 / 0.0. Gemini-1.5-Pro without perception -19.5 / -20.8 / -2.0 (column alignment of this row is uncertain).
limits: Three models; ToM only; some cells missing in the extracted table.
agent_relevance: Gap 10: the step that infers what the agent perceived before judging the action is the key one. Supports a 'what was visible to X' step inside each scope. Self-correction not useful.

source: Liang et al. (2025) LLM-Hanabi: ToM and rationale inference in an imperfect-information game
finding: In a 5-player cooperative game, first-order ToM scores exceed second-order for every model, and first-order tracks game success more.
numbers: Table 1, first/second-order ToM (0-100 LLM judge): DeepSeek-R1 87.05/68.31 (game 30.00); GPT-4.1 83.81/72.46 (28.56); Gemini-2.5-Flash 86.67/67.13 (25.04); Llama-3.1-8B 61.98/20.71 (3.47). Correlation with game score r=0.76 (first-order) and 0.58 (second-order). 30-50 games per model, temperature 0.7.
limits: LLM-as-judge scoring; no CIs; the paper has internal inconsistencies in the score scale.
agent_relevance: Gap 8: second-order costs 10 to 20 points for most current models and 40 for an 8B model. Depth is a gradient, not a cliff.

source: Laban et al. (2025) LLMs Get Lost In Multi-Turn Conversation
finding: Early assumptions persist and contaminate later turns: when a model takes a wrong turn it does not recover. Average drop 39% over six tasks; mostly unreliability, little aptitude loss.
numbers: 200,000+ simulated conversations, six generation tasks, many open and closed models (names not on the page read).
limits: Abstract only. Not a spaces study; the link to leakage is by analogy. Does not vary the number of spaces.
agent_relevance: Gap 3 not closed. Indirect support that unrevised early content leaks forward, and that a scaffold should restate or reset scoped state.

source: Nieuwland & Martin (2012) If the real world were irrelevant, so to speak
finding: ERP. In counterfactual sentences, false words elicit larger N400 than true words, the same as in real-world sentences. No delay from real-world knowledge. Humans map words onto the counterfactual world at once.
numbers: N400 truth-value effects in counterfactual and real-world sentences are described as indistinguishable. Abstract gives no N or amplitudes; not extracted.
limits: Abstract only (PubMed). Sample size and microvolt effects not read. Tone conflicts with the Ferguson-lab switching cost (d17) and Kulakova & Nieuwland (d16).
agent_relevance: Gap 7 partly: little or no leakage in humans when the context is constraining. The agent target is that scoped content gets no reality interference.

source: Kulakova & Nieuwland (2016) Pragmatic skills predict online counterfactual comprehension: Evidence from the N400
finding: Full text read. Words true in the real world but placed in counterfactual antecedents carry a processing cost (bigger N400) versus hypothetical antecedents, so real-world expectations are reduced but a cost remains. Pragmatic skill (AQ Communication) moderates it.
numbers: 30 Edinburgh students recruited (df = 22 in the ANOVAs); 90 sentences. Truth-value main effect 1.16 microvolt, F(1,22)=14.10, p<.001, partial eta-squared .39. Mood main effect 0.72 microvolt, F(1,22)=8.44, p<.01, eta-sq .28. Truth x mood x hemisphere F(1,22)=13.42, eta-sq .39. Cloze: true .30/.31 vs false .04/.02, F(1,89)=125.75; cloze from 81 raters.
limits: Compares counterfactual with hypothetical, not with a pure real-world control. Single lab.
agent_relevance: Gap 7: humans carry a measurable but small leakage in counterfactual spaces, about 0.7 microvolt. A scope cue (mood) works quickly; an explicit space label should be the analogue.

source: Autistic adults are not impaired at maintaining or switching between counterfactual and factual worlds (2022, Ferguson-lab ERP)
finding: ERP study built on Ferguson & Cane (2015) with 24 autistic and 24 typical adults. Maintaining a counterfactual world is easy. Switching back from a counterfactual to a factual world shows early interference from the counterfactual context, then later recovery.
numbers: N=48 (24+24; one extra autistic participant excluded for noise). About 28-29 of 30 trials kept per condition. In the counterfactual-to-factual switch, the consistency N400 effect was not significant early and appeared later over posterior electrodes. No group effects despite group ToM and flexibility differences.
limits: Effect sizes for the switch condition not extracted. Interference is early and temporary. First author not read from the page.
agent_relevance: Gap 7: the leakage humans show is at exits from a space (switching back). Our scaffold should make the exit step explicit: close the space and restate the base state.

source: Coulson & Van Petten (2002) Conceptual integration and metaphor: an event-related potential study
finding: ERP, 18 adults. N400 smallest for literal endings, largest for metaphors, intermediate for literal-mapping endings (literal sense used with a cross-domain mapping). Metaphors also gave a larger posterior positivity. Read as a cost of conceptual integration, as blending theory predicts.
numbers: N=18; N400 window 300-500 ms. Abstract gives no microvolt values or test statistics.
limits: Abstract only. Amplitudes not read. The cost ordering could also reflect cloze or familiarity differences.
agent_relevance: Gap 7: confirms blending has a processing cost in humans (supports K18). Effect sizes still missing.

source: Lynn (2026) Conceptual blending in humans and language models
finding: Conceptual analysis of goal-directed blending in brains (predictive processing) versus LLMs (proxy-goals from alignment and prompt). Toy example only; no measured blending prompt method. Cites two 2025 works (Peng et al., Sato) saying LLMs blend, but these were not located.
numbers: No empirical data. A vector-symbolic toy script is in the supplement.
limits: Conceptual paper by an agent-design group; the cited LLM blending studies were not opened.
agent_relevance: Gap 9 stays open: no measured gain from blending as a prompt method was found. Keep blends out of the schema (SCHEMA section 4b).
